# Exercise 4.2 — The decision boundary {#sec-decision-boundary}

In Exercise 4.1 the map of the logistic regression's probability had a black
line across it: to one side the model says `yes`, to the other `no`. That line
is the **decision boundary**. In this exercise you work it out from the
coefficients, see why it is straight, move it with the threshold, and meet data
where no straight line can do the job.

Parts 1 and 2 use the same people as Exercise 4.1: age, systolic blood
pressure, and whether they had a cardiovascular event in the next ten years.
Both measurements matter, so the boundary is tilted.

- **Part 1.** Find the boundary by hand from the coefficients, draw it, and
  see it as the line where a plane is cut, in 3D.
- **Part 2.** Change the threshold and see the line move: every threshold
  gives its own line.
- **Part 3.** A dataset where the risk is high at both ends of a measurement.
  A straight boundary fails; a squared term or a tree gives a boundary that
  bends.

::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}
## The plots are for looking at
The code for the plots is folded away under **Code for this plot

:::

### Packages and data

```{r}
# Packages for this exercise. If one is missing, remove the # and run this line once:
# install.packages(c("tidyverse", "tidymodels", "plotly"))

library(tidyverse)
library(tidymodels)

theme_set(theme_bw())
```

`data/cvd_risk.csv` holds 500 adults aged 40 to 80 seen at a health check:
their age, their systolic blood pressure in mmHg, and whether they had a
cardiovascular event (a heart attack or a stroke) in the following ten years.
If you do not have it yet, [**download `cvd_risk.csv`**](data/cvd_risk.csv){download="cvd_risk.csv"}
into your `data` folder.

```{r}
cvd <- read_csv("data/cvd_risk.csv") |>
  mutate(cvd = factor(cvd, levels = c("no", "yes")))

test_rows <- seq(1, nrow(cvd), by = 5)     # every fifth person is held back
train <- cvd[-test_rows, ]
test  <- cvd[test_rows, ]

count(train, cvd)
```

### Part 1 — Where the class changes

Fit a logistic regression with both measurements, the same way as in
Exercise 4.1:

```{r}
log_model <- logistic_reg() |>
  set_engine("glm") |>
  set_mode("classification")

log_fit <- log_model |>
  fit(cvd ~ age + systolic_bp, data = train)

b <- log_fit$fit$coefficients      # intercept, age, blood pressure
b
```

The model is a straight line on the **log-odds** scale. Log-odds are another
way of writing a probability $p$: $\log\big(p / (1 - p)\big)$. A probability of
0.5 has log-odds 0; higher probabilities have positive log-odds, lower ones
negative. The sigmoid turns log-odds back into a probability.


$$\text{log-odds} = \beta_0 + \beta_1 \times \text{age} + \beta_2 \times \text{blood pressure}$$

By default the model says `yes` when the probability is 0.5 or more. At 0.5
the probability is shared equally between the two classes: 0.5 for an event and
0.5 for no event. Above it `yes` is the more likely class, below it `no`. So
the class changes where the probability is 0.5, which is **log-odds of 0**. So the boundary is every
combination of age and blood pressure where

$$\beta_0 + \beta_1 \times \text{age} + \beta_2 \times \text{blood pressure} = 0$$

For a given blood pressure, solve for age:

$$\text{age} = \frac{-\beta_0 - \beta_2 \times \text{blood pressure}}{\beta_1}$$

#### Task 1a — The boundary at a blood pressure of 120 and of 160

Round the coefficients printed above to four significant figures and calculate,
by hand, the age at which the class changes for a blood pressure of 120 mmHg.
Then do the same for 160 mmHg.

```{r}
#| eval: false
# Replace every ______ below, then run this cell.
boundary_120 <- (-(______) - ______ * 120) / ______
boundary_160 <- (-(______) - ______ * 160) / ______
c(boundary_120, boundary_160)
```

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Stuck?
In order: the intercept, the blood-pressure weight, and the age weight. The
intercept is negative, so minus the intercept is a positive number.
:::

::: {.content-visible when-meta="show-solutions"}
::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}
## Worked answer
```{r}
boundary_120 <- (-(-14.22) - 0.05292 * 120) / 0.1042
boundary_160 <- (-(-14.22) - 0.05292 * 160) / 0.1042
c(boundary_120, boundary_160)
```

With a blood pressure of 120 the model predicts an event from about age 76;
with 160, from about age 55.
:::
:::

Check it with `predict()`: a person on the boundary should get a probability
of 0.5.

```{r}
predict(log_fit, new_data = data.frame(age = 75.6, systolic_bp = 120), type = "prob")
```

Every point on the boundary satisfies one linear equation in age and blood
pressure, so the boundary is a **straight line**. Here it is, drawn from the
coefficients, over the test patients:

```{r}
#| code-fold: true
#| code-summary: "Code for this plot (optional)"
# the boundary written as blood pressure = a + s * age
ggplot(test, aes(x = age, y = systolic_bp, shape = cvd, colour = cvd)) +
  geom_point(size = 2) +
  geom_abline(intercept = -b[1] / b[3], slope = -b[2] / b[3], linewidth = 1) +
  annotate("point", x = c(75.6, 55.3), y = c(120, 160), colour = "red", size = 3) +
  scale_shape_manual(values = c(no = 1, yes = 17)) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c(no = "steelblue", yes = "darkorange")) +
  coord_cartesian(xlim = c(40, 80), ylim = c(80, 200)) +
  labs(x = "Age (years)", y = "Systolic blood pressure (mmHg)",
       shape = "Event", colour = "Event",
       title = "The decision boundary at a threshold of 0.5")
```

Above and to the right of the line the model says `yes`; below and to the left,
`no`. The line is tilted because both measurements count: an older person
needs a lower blood pressure to cross it.

#### The same line in three dimensions

The log-odds, $\beta_0 + \beta_1 \times \text{age} + \beta_2 \times \text{blood pressure}$,
are a flat, tilted **plane** above the age–blood pressure floor, like the plane
in Exercise 3.1. The grey sheet is height 0. Where the plane passes through the
sheet is the decision boundary, the black line: where the plane is above the
sheet the model says `yes`, where it is below, `no`. The test patients are drawn
on the grey sheet. Turn the plot with the mouse and scroll to zoom.

```{r}
#| code-fold: true
#| code-summary: "Code for this plot (optional)"
#| eval: !expr requireNamespace("plotly", quietly = TRUE)
# This plot needs the plotly package: install.packages("plotly")
ages <- seq(40, 80, by = 1)
bps  <- seq(80, 200, by = 2)

# the log-odds at every grid point: one row per blood pressure, one column per age
logodds_matrix <- outer(bps, ages, function(s, a) b[1] + b[2] * a + b[3] * s)

# the boundary: the age where the log-odds are 0, for each blood pressure
line_age <- (-b[1] - b[3] * bps) / b[2]
on_floor <- line_age >= 40 & line_age <= 80

no  <- filter(test, cvd == "no")
yes <- filter(test, cvd == "yes")

plotly::plot_ly() |>
  plotly::add_surface(x = ages, y = bps, z = logodds_matrix, opacity = 0.75,
                      colorscale = list(c(0, 1), c("steelblue", "darkorange")),
                      showscale = FALSE, name = "log-odds") |>
  plotly::add_surface(x = ages, y = bps, z = 0 * logodds_matrix, opacity = 0.4,
                      colorscale = list(c(0, 1), c("grey", "grey")),
                      showscale = FALSE, name = "height 0") |>
  plotly::add_trace(type = "scatter3d", mode = "lines", x = line_age[on_floor],
                    y = bps[on_floor], z = rep(0, sum(on_floor)),
                    line = list(color = "black", width = 8), name = "boundary") |>
  plotly::add_trace(type = "scatter3d", mode = "markers", x = no$age, y = no$systolic_bp,
                    z = rep(0, nrow(no)), marker = list(size = 3, color = "steelblue"),
                    name = "test: no") |>
  plotly::add_trace(type = "scatter3d", mode = "markers", x = yes$age, y = yes$systolic_bp,
                    z = rep(0, nrow(yes)), marker = list(size = 3, color = "darkorange"),
                    name = "test: yes") |>
  plotly::layout(scene = list(xaxis = list(title = "Age (years)"),
                              yaxis = list(title = "Systolic BP (mmHg)"),
                              zaxis = list(title = "Log-odds of an event")))
```

The sigmoid turns each log-odds into a probability, which bends the flat plane
into an S-shaped sheet between 0 and 1. A log-odds of 0 is a probability of
0.5, so the sheet crosses the grey level at 0.5 along exactly the same black
line. The test patients sit at 1 (an event) and at 0 (no event). Click
**level 0.3** and **level 0.7** in the legend to show two more levels; Part 2
is about them.

```{r}
#| code-fold: true
#| code-summary: "Code for this plot (optional)"
#| eval: !expr requireNamespace("plotly", quietly = TRUE)
# the probability at every grid point: the sigmoid of the log-odds
prob_matrix <- 1 / (1 + exp(-logodds_matrix))

fig_prob <- plotly::plot_ly() |>
  plotly::add_surface(x = ages, y = bps, z = prob_matrix, opacity = 0.75,
                      colorscale = list(c(0, 1), c("steelblue", "darkorange")),
                      showscale = FALSE, name = "probability")
for (t in c(0.3, 0.5, 0.7)) {
  fig_prob <- fig_prob |>
    plotly::add_surface(x = ages, y = bps, z = 0 * prob_matrix + t, opacity = 0.4,
                        colorscale = list(c(0, 1), c("grey", "grey")), showscale = FALSE,
                        showlegend = TRUE, name = paste("level", t),
                        visible = if (t == 0.5) TRUE else "legendonly")
}
fig_prob |>
  plotly::add_trace(type = "scatter3d", mode = "lines", x = line_age[on_floor],
                    y = bps[on_floor], z = rep(0.5, sum(on_floor)),
                    line = list(color = "black", width = 8), name = "boundary at 0.5") |>
  plotly::add_trace(type = "scatter3d", mode = "markers", x = no$age, y = no$systolic_bp,
                    z = rep(0, nrow(no)), marker = list(size = 3, color = "steelblue"),
                    name = "test: no") |>
  plotly::add_trace(type = "scatter3d", mode = "markers", x = yes$age, y = yes$systolic_bp,
                    z = rep(1, nrow(yes)), marker = list(size = 3, color = "darkorange"),
                    name = "test: yes") |>
  plotly::layout(scene = list(xaxis = list(title = "Age (years)"),
                              yaxis = list(title = "Systolic BP (mmHg)"),
                              zaxis = list(title = "Probability of an event")))
```

```{r}
#| echo: false
if (!requireNamespace("plotly", quietly = TRUE)) knitr::asis_output(paste0(
  "*The plots you can turn are missing from this copy of the page: they need the R ",
  "package `plotly`. Run `install.packages(\"plotly\")` and render again.*"))
```

::: {.callout-important appearance="simple"}
## Think about it
1. As far as the model is concerned, 10 mmHg more blood pressure is worth how
   many years of age? Where do you see that in the plot?
2. Two people: one is 70 with a blood pressure of 130, the other 55 with 165.
   Which side of the line is each on?
3. A model with three predictors (say age, blood pressure and cholesterol) also
   has a boundary. What shape would it be?
:::

::: {.content-visible when-meta="show-solutions"}
::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}
## Worked answer
```{r}
predict(log_fit, new_data = data.frame(age = c(70, 55), systolic_bp = c(130, 165)),
        type = "prob")
```

1. About 5 years: 10 × 0.0529 / 0.1042 = 5.1. Adding 10 mmHg raises the
   log-odds as much as 5 extra years. That is the tilt of the line: going 10
   mmHg up, the boundary moves 5 years younger (from 76 at 120 mmHg to 55 at
   160 mmHg).
2. The 70-year-old is just below the line (probability 0.49, `no`); the
   55-year-old is above it (0.56, `yes`). The younger person is called `yes`
   because of the blood pressure. Neither measurement decides alone.
3. Still flat: one linear equation in three measurements is a flat plane in
   three dimensions. A logistic regression always has a flat boundary in the
   predictors you give it.
:::
:::

### Part 2 — The threshold moves the line

The cut-off of 0.5 is called the **decision threshold**. Nothing forces it to
be 0.5: we could call someone `yes` from a probability of 0.3, or only from
0.7. A threshold $t$ is a probability, so it has
a log-odds, $\log\big(t / (1 - t)\big)$, and the boundary is where the model's
log-odds equal it:

$$\beta_0 + \beta_1 \times \text{age} + \beta_2 \times \text{blood pressure} = \log\left(\frac{t}{1-t}\right)$$

Only the right-hand side changes, so the line keeps its tilt and moves
sideways. In the 3D plot of Part 1 this is cutting the S-shaped sheet at a
different height: the 0.3 level meets it further down and to the left, the 0.7
level further up and to the right.

#### Task 2a — The log-odds of three thresholds

```{r}
#| eval: false
# Replace every ______ below, then run this cell.
thresholds <- data.frame(t = c(0.3, 0.5, 0.7)) |>
  mutate(log_odds = log(______ / (1 - ______)),
         age_at_bp_140 = (log_odds - b[1] - b[3] * 140) / b[2])

thresholds
```

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Stuck?
Both blanks are the threshold column, `t`.
:::

::: {.content-visible when-meta="show-solutions"}
::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}
## Worked answer
```{r}
thresholds <- data.frame(t = c(0.3, 0.5, 0.7)) |>
  mutate(log_odds = log(t / (1 - t)),
         age_at_bp_140 = (log_odds - b[1] - b[3] * 140) / b[2])

thresholds
```

The log-odds are −0.847, 0 and 0.847. For a blood pressure of 140 the class
changes at age 57, 65 and 74.
:::
:::

```{r}
#| code-fold: true
#| code-summary: "Code for this plot (optional)"
lines_t <- data.frame(t = factor(c(0.3, 0.5, 0.7)),
                      log_odds = log(c(0.3, 0.5, 0.7) / (1 - c(0.3, 0.5, 0.7)))) |>
  mutate(intercept = (log_odds - b[1]) / b[3], slope = -b[2] / b[3])

ggplot(test, aes(x = age, y = systolic_bp)) +
  geom_point(aes(shape = cvd), size = 2, colour = "grey30") +
  geom_abline(data = lines_t, aes(intercept = intercept, slope = slope, colour = t),
              linewidth = 1) +
  scale_shape_manual(values = c(no = 1, yes = 17)) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c("0.3" = "blue", "0.5" = "red", "0.7" = "purple")) +
  coord_cartesian(xlim = c(40, 80), ylim = c(80, 200)) +
  labs(x = "Age (years)", y = "Systolic blood pressure (mmHg)",
       shape = "Event", colour = "Threshold",
       title = "Three thresholds, three parallel boundaries")
```

::: {.callout-important}
## Key idea
We could have picked another threshold, and we would have had a different line
separating our classes in 2D: one line for each threshold. The 0.5 line,
where both classes are equally likely, is only the default.
:::

Everyone above a line is predicted `yes` at that threshold. Count them:

```{r}
test_probs <- predict(log_fit, new_data = test, type = "prob")$.pred_yes

c(t_0.3 = sum(test_probs >= 0.3), t_0.5 = sum(test_probs >= 0.5),
  t_0.7 = sum(test_probs >= 0.7))
```

::: {.callout-important appearance="simple"}
## Think about it
Lowering the threshold from 0.5 to 0.3 calls many more test patients `yes`.
On the plot, which patients change side when the line moves from 0.5 to 0.3:
triangles (they had an event), circles (they did not), or both?
:::

::: {.content-visible when-meta="show-solutions"}
::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}
## Worked answer
52 patients are called `yes` at 0.3, 31 at 0.5 and 15 at 0.7. Moving the line
down (0.3) brings more of the triangles onto the `yes` side, but it brings over
circles too. Moving it up (0.7) does the opposite: fewer circles called `yes`,
but more triangles missed. The model, its coefficients and the tilt of the line
are the same; only the decision changed. Why you might want to move it is the
subject of Exercise 4.3.
:::
:::

### Part 3 — When a straight line cannot work

`data/sodium_delirium.csv` holds 500 older patients admitted to hospital: their
age, their blood sodium in mmol/L (normal is about 135 to 145), and whether
they developed delirium during the admission. If you do not have it yet,
[**download `sodium_delirium.csv`**](data/sodium_delirium.csv){download="sodium_delirium.csv"}
into your `data` folder.

```{r}
delirium <- read_csv("data/sodium_delirium.csv") |>
  mutate(delirium = factor(delirium, levels = c("no", "yes")))

test_rows_d <- seq(1, nrow(delirium), by = 5)     # every fifth patient is held back
train_d <- delirium[-test_rows_d, ]
test_d  <- delirium[test_rows_d, ]

count(train_d, delirium)
```

```{r}
#| code-fold: true
#| code-summary: "Code for this plot (optional)"
ggplot(train_d, aes(x = sodium, y = age, shape = delirium, colour = delirium)) +
  geom_point(size = 2) +
  scale_shape_manual(values = c(no = 1, yes = 17)) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c(no = "steelblue", yes = "darkorange")) +
  labs(x = "Sodium (mmol/L)", y = "Age (years)", shape = "Delirium", colour = "Delirium",
       title = "Training patients")
```

Delirium is common when sodium is **too low and when it is too high**, and
rarer in between. Fit the same kind of model as before, with age and sodium:

```{r}
line_fit <- log_model |>
  fit(delirium ~ age + sodium, data = train_d)

line_fit$fit$coefficients
```

```{r}
#| code-fold: true
#| code-summary: "Code for this plot (optional)"
grid_d <- expand_grid(sodium = seq(114, 163, by = 0.5), age = seq(60, 98, by = 0.5)) |>
  mutate(sodium_dev2 = (sodium - 140)^2)

delirium_map <- function(fit, title) {
  grid_d$prob <- predict(fit, new_data = grid_d, type = "prob")$.pred_yes
  ggplot(grid_d, aes(x = sodium, y = age)) +
    geom_raster(aes(fill = prob)) +
    geom_contour(aes(z = prob), breaks = 0.5, colour = "black", linewidth = 0.8) +
    geom_point(data = test_d, aes(shape = delirium), size = 1.5) +
    scale_fill_gradient2(low = "steelblue", mid = "white", high = "darkorange",
                         midpoint = 0.5, limits = c(0, 1)) +
    scale_shape_manual(values = c(no = 1, yes = 17)) +
    labs(x = "Sodium (mmol/L)", y = "Age (years)",
         fill = "Probability\nof delirium", shape = "Test patients", title = title)
}

delirium_map(line_fit, "Logistic regression: age + sodium")
```

The weight for sodium is almost exactly 0, and the map has no boundary at all:
the probability never reaches 0.5, so the model says `no` for every patient.
A straight line has to put "high risk" on one side. Here the high-risk patients
are on **both** sides, so the best straight line the model can find is one that
hardly uses sodium.

#### Task 3a — Give the model a predictor it can use

How far sodium is from normal matters, not which direction. Make a new column,
the squared distance from 140, and add it to the model. The model is still a
logistic regression, linear in the predictors you give it, but one of those
predictors is now curved in sodium.

```{r}
#| eval: false
# Replace every ______ below, then run this cell.
train_d <- train_d |> mutate(sodium_dev2 = (sodium - 140)^2)
test_d  <- test_d  |> mutate(sodium_dev2 = (sodium - 140)^2)

curve_fit <- log_model |>
  fit(delirium ~ age + sodium + ______, data = train_d)

curve_fit$fit$coefficients
```

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Stuck?
Add the name of the new column to the formula, after a `+`.
:::

::: {.content-visible when-meta="show-solutions"}
::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}
## Worked answer
```{r}
train_d <- train_d |> mutate(sodium_dev2 = (sodium - 140)^2)
test_d  <- test_d  |> mutate(sodium_dev2 = (sodium - 140)^2)

curve_fit <- log_model |>
  fit(delirium ~ age + sodium + sodium_dev2, data = train_d)

curve_fit$fit$coefficients
```

The weight for `sodium_dev2` is positive (0.023): the further sodium is from
140, in either direction, the higher the log-odds of delirium. Age now has a
clear positive weight too (0.039).
:::
:::

```{r}
#| code-fold: true
#| code-summary: "Code for this plot (optional)"
delirium_map(curve_fit, "Logistic regression: age + sodium + (sodium - 140)²")
```

A tree needs no new column: it can split on sodium twice.

```{r}
tree_fit <- decision_tree() |>
  set_engine("rpart") |>
  set_mode("classification") |>
  fit(delirium ~ age + sodium, data = train_d)

tree_fit
```

```{r}
#| code-fold: true
#| code-summary: "Code for this plot (optional)"
delirium_map(tree_fit, "Decision tree: age + sodium")
```

How often is each model right on the 100 test patients, and what does each say
about an 80-year-old with a low, a normal and a high sodium?

```{r}
data.frame(
  model = c("straight line", "with (sodium - 140)²", "tree", "always says no"),
  accuracy = c(mean(predict(line_fit,  new_data = test_d)$.pred_class == test_d$delirium),
               mean(predict(curve_fit, new_data = test_d)$.pred_class == test_d$delirium),
               mean(predict(tree_fit,  new_data = test_d)$.pred_class == test_d$delirium),
               mean(test_d$delirium == "no")))

patients <- data.frame(age = 80, sodium = c(126, 140, 154)) |>
  mutate(sodium_dev2 = (sodium - 140)^2)

patients |>
  mutate(straight_line = predict(line_fit,  new_data = patients, type = "prob")$.pred_yes,
         with_squared  = predict(curve_fit, new_data = patients, type = "prob")$.pred_yes,
         tree          = predict(tree_fit,  new_data = patients, type = "prob")$.pred_yes)
```

::: {.callout-important appearance="simple"}
## Think about it
1. The straight-line model is right for 72% of the test patients. Is that a
   good model?
2. The straight-line model says sodium hardly matters. Is that true?
3. Describe the boundary of the model with the squared term, and of the tree.
:::

::: {.content-visible when-meta="show-solutions"}
::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}
## Worked answer
1. No. Always saying `no` is also right for 72%: the model says `no` to
   everyone and has learned nothing useful. Compare every accuracy with that
   baseline.
2. No. Sodium matters a great deal, but in both directions, which a straight
   line cannot express. An 80-year-old gets 0.33, 0.32 and 0.31 from the
   straight line whatever their sodium; the model with the squared term gives
   0.88, 0.08 and 0.91. A weight near 0 means "no straight-line relationship",
   not "no relationship".
3. The squared term gives two curved lines: delirium is predicted when sodium
   is below about 130 or above about 150, and the normal band narrows slightly
   with age (about 128 to 151 at 65, about 131 to 149 at 95). The tree gives
   three vertical bands: sodium below 130.5, 130.5 to 149.5, and 149.5 or
   above; it does not use age at all. Both are right for 88% of the test
   patients.
:::
:::

::: {.callout-important}
## Learning points
- The decision boundary is where the predicted probability equals the
  threshold. For a logistic regression that is where the log-odds equal
  $\log\big(t/(1-t)\big)$: 0 for a threshold of 0.5.
- A logistic regression's boundary is straight (flat) in its predictors.
  Changing the threshold moves it without changing its tilt.
- When the risk is high at both ends of a measurement, no straight line can
  separate the classes, and a weight near 0 can hide a strong relationship.
- A boundary can bend if you give the model a curved predictor, such as a
  squared term, or use a model that bends on its own, such as a tree.
:::

### Packages and data

```{python}
# Packages for this exercise. If one is missing, install it once from a terminal
# (in a Jupyter notebook, type %pip instead of pip):
# pip install pandas numpy matplotlib scikit-learn plotly

import pandas as pd
import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

from sklearn.linear_model import LogisticRegression
from sklearn.tree import DecisionTreeClassifier, export_text
```

`data/cvd_risk.csv` holds 500 adults aged 40 to 80 seen at a health check:
their age, their systolic blood pressure in mmHg, and whether they had a
cardiovascular event (a heart attack or a stroke) in the following ten years.
If you do not have it yet, [**download `cvd_risk.csv`**](data/cvd_risk.csv){download="cvd_risk.csv"}
into your `data` folder.

```{python}
cvd = pd.read_csv("data/cvd_risk.csv")

is_test = cvd.index % 5 == 0               # every fifth person is held back
train = cvd[~is_test]
test  = cvd[is_test]

train["cvd"].value_counts()
```

### Part 1 — Where the class changes

Fit a logistic regression with both measurements, the same way as in
Exercise 4.1:

```{python}
log_model = LogisticRegression(C=np.inf)
log_model.fit(train[["age", "systolic_bp"]], train["cvd"])

b0 = log_model.intercept_[0]
b1, b2 = log_model.coef_[0]          # age, blood pressure
print("intercept:", b0)
print("weights (age, blood pressure):", b1, b2)
```

The model is a straight line on the **log-odds** scale. Log-odds are another
way of writing a probability $p$: $\log\big(p / (1 - p)\big)$. A probability of
0.5 has log-odds 0; higher probabilities have positive log-odds, lower ones
negative. The sigmoid turns log-odds back into a probability.


$$\text{log-odds} = \beta_0 + \beta_1 \times \text{age} + \beta_2 \times \text{blood pressure}$$

By default the model says `yes` when the probability is 0.5 or more. At 0.5
the probability is shared equally between the two classes: 0.5 for an event and
0.5 for no event. Above it `yes` is the more likely class, below it `no`. So
the class changes where the probability is 0.5, which is **log-odds of 0**. So the boundary is every
combination of age and blood pressure where

$$\beta_0 + \beta_1 \times \text{age} + \beta_2 \times \text{blood pressure} = 0$$

For a given blood pressure, solve for age:

$$\text{age} = \frac{-\beta_0 - \beta_2 \times \text{blood pressure}}{\beta_1}$$

#### Task 1a — The boundary at a blood pressure of 120 and of 160

Round the coefficients printed above to four significant figures and calculate,
by hand, the age at which the class changes for a blood pressure of 120 mmHg.
Then do the same for 160 mmHg.

```{python}
#| eval: false
# Replace every ______ below, then run this cell.
boundary_120 = (-(______) - ______ * 120) / ______
boundary_160 = (-(______) - ______ * 160) / ______
print(boundary_120, boundary_160)
```

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Stuck?
In order: the intercept, the blood-pressure weight, and the age weight. The
intercept is negative, so minus the intercept is a positive number.
:::

::: {.content-visible when-meta="show-solutions"}
::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}
## Worked answer
```{python}
boundary_120 = (-(-14.22) - 0.05292 * 120) / 0.1042
boundary_160 = (-(-14.22) - 0.05292 * 160) / 0.1042
print(boundary_120, boundary_160)
```

With a blood pressure of 120 the model predicts an event from about age 76;
with 160, from about age 55.
:::
:::

Check it with `.predict_proba()`: a person on the boundary should get a
probability of 0.5.

```{python}
log_model.predict_proba(pd.DataFrame({"age": [75.6], "systolic_bp": [120]}))
```

Every point on the boundary satisfies one linear equation in age and blood
pressure, so the boundary is a **straight line**. Here it is, drawn from the
coefficients, over the test patients:

```{python}
#| code-fold: true
#| code-summary: "Code for this plot (optional)"
age_line = np.array([40, 80])
fig, ax = plt.subplots()
for cls, mk, colour in [("no", "o", "steelblue"), ("yes", "^", "darkorange")]:
    rows = test[test["cvd"] == cls]
    ax.scatter(rows["age"], rows["systolic_bp"], marker=mk, color=colour, s=20, label=cls)
# the boundary written as blood pressure = (-b0 - b1 * age) / b2
ax.plot(age_line, (-b0 - b1 * age_line) / b2, color="black", linewidth=2)
ax.scatter([75.6, 55.3], [120, 160], color="red", s=50, zorder=3)
ax.set_xlim(40, 80)
ax.set_ylim(80, 200)
ax.set_xlabel("Age (years)")
ax.set_ylabel("Systolic blood pressure (mmHg)")
ax.legend(title="Event")
ax.set_title("The decision boundary at a threshold of 0.5")
plt.show()
```

Above and to the right of the line the model says `yes`; below and to the left,
`no`. The line is tilted because both measurements count: an older person
needs a lower blood pressure to cross it.

#### The same line in three dimensions

The log-odds, $\beta_0 + \beta_1 \times \text{age} + \beta_2 \times \text{blood pressure}$,
are a flat, tilted **plane** above the age–blood pressure floor, like the plane
in Exercise 3.1. The grey sheet is height 0. Where the plane passes through the
sheet is the decision boundary, the black line: where the plane is above the
sheet the model says `yes`, where it is below, `no`. The test patients are drawn
on the grey sheet. Turn the plot with the mouse and scroll to zoom.

```{python}
#| code-fold: true
#| code-summary: "Code for this plot (optional)"
#| eval: false
# This plot needs the plotly package: pip install plotly
import plotly.graph_objects as go

ages = np.arange(40, 81, 1)
bps = np.arange(80, 201, 2)
A, S = np.meshgrid(ages, bps)

# the log-odds at every grid point: one row per blood pressure, one column per age
logodds_matrix = b0 + b1 * A + b2 * S

# the boundary: the age where the log-odds are 0, for each blood pressure
line_age = (-b0 - b2 * bps) / b1
on_floor = (line_age >= 40) & (line_age <= 80)

no = test[test["cvd"] == "no"]
yes = test[test["cvd"] == "yes"]

fig_logodds = go.Figure()
fig_logodds.add_trace(go.Surface(x=ages, y=bps, z=logodds_matrix, opacity=0.75,
    colorscale=[[0, "steelblue"], [1, "darkorange"]], showscale=False, name="log-odds"))
fig_logodds.add_trace(go.Surface(x=ages, y=bps, z=0 * logodds_matrix, opacity=0.4,
    colorscale=[[0, "grey"], [1, "grey"]], showscale=False, name="height 0"))
fig_logodds.add_trace(go.Scatter3d(x=line_age[on_floor], y=bps[on_floor],
    z=np.zeros(on_floor.sum()), mode="lines", line={"color": "black", "width": 8},
    name="boundary"))
fig_logodds.add_trace(go.Scatter3d(x=no["age"], y=no["systolic_bp"], z=np.zeros(len(no)),
    mode="markers", marker={"size": 3, "color": "steelblue"}, name="test: no"))
fig_logodds.add_trace(go.Scatter3d(x=yes["age"], y=yes["systolic_bp"], z=np.zeros(len(yes)),
    mode="markers", marker={"size": 3, "color": "darkorange"}, name="test: yes"))
fig_logodds.update_layout(scene={"xaxis_title": "Age (years)",
                                 "yaxis_title": "Systolic BP (mmHg)",
                                 "zaxis_title": "Log-odds of an event"})
fig_logodds.show()
```

The sigmoid turns each log-odds into a probability, which bends the flat plane
into an S-shaped sheet between 0 and 1. A log-odds of 0 is a probability of
0.5, so the sheet crosses the grey level at 0.5 along exactly the same black
line. The test patients sit at 1 (an event) and at 0 (no event). Click
**level 0.3** and **level 0.7** in the legend to show two more levels; Part 2
is about them.

```{python}
#| code-fold: true
#| code-summary: "Code for this plot (optional)"
#| eval: false
# the probability at every grid point: the sigmoid of the log-odds
prob_matrix = 1 / (1 + np.exp(-logodds_matrix))

fig_prob = go.Figure()
fig_prob.add_trace(go.Surface(x=ages, y=bps, z=prob_matrix, opacity=0.75,
    colorscale=[[0, "steelblue"], [1, "darkorange"]], showscale=False, name="probability"))
for t in [0.3, 0.5, 0.7]:
    fig_prob.add_trace(go.Surface(x=ages, y=bps, z=0 * prob_matrix + t, opacity=0.4,
        colorscale=[[0, "grey"], [1, "grey"]], showscale=False, showlegend=True,
        name=f"level {t}", visible=True if t == 0.5 else "legendonly"))
fig_prob.add_trace(go.Scatter3d(x=line_age[on_floor], y=bps[on_floor],
    z=np.full(on_floor.sum(), 0.5), mode="lines", line={"color": "black", "width": 8},
    name="boundary at 0.5"))
fig_prob.add_trace(go.Scatter3d(x=no["age"], y=no["systolic_bp"], z=np.zeros(len(no)),
    mode="markers", marker={"size": 3, "color": "steelblue"}, name="test: no"))
fig_prob.add_trace(go.Scatter3d(x=yes["age"], y=yes["systolic_bp"], z=np.ones(len(yes)),
    mode="markers", marker={"size": 3, "color": "darkorange"}, name="test: yes"))
fig_prob.update_layout(scene={"xaxis_title": "Age (years)",
                              "yaxis_title": "Systolic BP (mmHg)",
                              "zaxis_title": "Probability of an event"})
fig_prob.show()
```

::: {.callout-important appearance="simple"}
## Think about it
1. As far as the model is concerned, 10 mmHg more blood pressure is worth how
   many years of age? Where do you see that in the plot?
2. Two people: one is 70 with a blood pressure of 130, the other 55 with 165.
   Which side of the line is each on?
3. A model with three predictors (say age, blood pressure and cholesterol) also
   has a boundary. What shape would it be?
:::

::: {.content-visible when-meta="show-solutions"}
::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}
## Worked answer
```{python}
log_model.predict_proba(pd.DataFrame({"age": [70, 55], "systolic_bp": [130, 165]}))
```

1. About 5 years: 10 × 0.0529 / 0.1042 = 5.1. Adding 10 mmHg raises the
   log-odds as much as 5 extra years. That is the tilt of the line: going 10
   mmHg up, the boundary moves 5 years younger (from 76 at 120 mmHg to 55 at
   160 mmHg).
2. The 70-year-old is just below the line (probability 0.49, `no`); the
   55-year-old is above it (0.56, `yes`). The younger person is called `yes`
   because of the blood pressure. Neither measurement decides alone.
3. Still flat: one linear equation in three measurements is a flat plane in
   three dimensions. A logistic regression always has a flat boundary in the
   predictors you give it.
:::
:::

### Part 2 — The threshold moves the line

The cut-off of 0.5 is called the **decision threshold**. Nothing forces it to
be 0.5: we could call someone `yes` from a probability of 0.3, or only from
0.7. A threshold $t$ is a probability, so it has
a log-odds, $\log\big(t / (1 - t)\big)$, and the boundary is where the model's
log-odds equal it:

$$\beta_0 + \beta_1 \times \text{age} + \beta_2 \times \text{blood pressure} = \log\left(\frac{t}{1-t}\right)$$

Only the right-hand side changes, so the line keeps its tilt and moves
sideways. In the 3D plot of Part 1 this is cutting the S-shaped sheet at a
different height: the 0.3 level meets it further down and to the left, the 0.7
level further up and to the right.

#### Task 2a — The log-odds of three thresholds

```{python}
#| eval: false
# Replace every ______ below, then run this cell.
thresholds = pd.DataFrame({"t": [0.3, 0.5, 0.7]})
thresholds["log_odds"] = np.log(______ / (1 - ______))
thresholds["age_at_bp_140"] = (thresholds["log_odds"] - b0 - b2 * 140) / b1

thresholds
```

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Stuck?
Both blanks are the threshold column, `thresholds["t"]`.
:::

::: {.content-visible when-meta="show-solutions"}
::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}
## Worked answer
```{python}
thresholds = pd.DataFrame({"t": [0.3, 0.5, 0.7]})
thresholds["log_odds"] = np.log(thresholds["t"] / (1 - thresholds["t"]))
thresholds["age_at_bp_140"] = (thresholds["log_odds"] - b0 - b2 * 140) / b1

thresholds
```

The log-odds are −0.847, 0 and 0.847. For a blood pressure of 140 the class
changes at age 57, 65 and 74.
:::
:::

```{python}
#| code-fold: true
#| code-summary: "Code for this plot (optional)"
fig, ax = plt.subplots()
for cls, mk in [("no", "o"), ("yes", "^")]:
    rows = test[test["cvd"] == cls]
    ax.scatter(rows["age"], rows["systolic_bp"], marker=mk, color="grey", s=20, label=cls)
for t, colour in [(0.3, "blue"), (0.5, "red"), (0.7, "purple")]:
    lo = np.log(t / (1 - t))
    ax.plot(age_line, (lo - b0 - b1 * age_line) / b2, color=colour,
            linewidth=2, label=f"threshold {t}")
ax.set_xlim(40, 80)
ax.set_ylim(80, 200)
ax.set_xlabel("Age (years)")
ax.set_ylabel("Systolic blood pressure (mmHg)")
ax.legend(fontsize=8)
ax.set_title("Three thresholds, three parallel boundaries")
plt.show()
```

::: {.callout-important}
## Key idea
We could have picked another threshold, and we would have had a different line
separating our classes in 2D: one line for each threshold. The 0.5 line,
where both classes are equally likely, is only the default.
:::

Everyone above a line is predicted `yes` at that threshold. Count them:

```{python}
test_probs = log_model.predict_proba(test[["age", "systolic_bp"]])[:, 1]

print("t = 0.3:", (test_probs >= 0.3).sum())
print("t = 0.5:", (test_probs >= 0.5).sum())
print("t = 0.7:", (test_probs >= 0.7).sum())
```

::: {.callout-important appearance="simple"}
## Think about it
Lowering the threshold from 0.5 to 0.3 calls many more test patients `yes`.
On the plot, which patients change side when the line moves from 0.5 to 0.3:
triangles (they had an event), circles (they did not), or both?
:::

::: {.content-visible when-meta="show-solutions"}
::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}
## Worked answer
52 patients are called `yes` at 0.3, 31 at 0.5 and 15 at 0.7. Moving the line
down (0.3) brings more of the triangles onto the `yes` side, but it brings over
circles too. Moving it up (0.7) does the opposite: fewer circles called `yes`,
but more triangles missed. The model, its coefficients and the tilt of the line
are the same; only the decision changed. Why you might want to move it is the
subject of Exercise 4.3.
:::
:::

### Part 3 — When a straight line cannot work

`data/sodium_delirium.csv` holds 500 older patients admitted to hospital: their
age, their blood sodium in mmol/L (normal is about 135 to 145), and whether
they developed delirium during the admission. If you do not have it yet,
[**download `sodium_delirium.csv`**](data/sodium_delirium.csv){download="sodium_delirium.csv"}
into your `data` folder.

```{python}
delirium = pd.read_csv("data/sodium_delirium.csv")

is_test_d = delirium.index % 5 == 0             # every fifth patient is held back
train_d = delirium[~is_test_d].copy()
test_d  = delirium[is_test_d].copy()

train_d["delirium"].value_counts()
```

```{python}
#| code-fold: true
#| code-summary: "Code for this plot (optional)"
fig, ax = plt.subplots()
for cls, mk, colour in [("no", "o", "steelblue"), ("yes", "^", "darkorange")]:
    rows = train_d[train_d["delirium"] == cls]
    ax.scatter(rows["sodium"], rows["age"], marker=mk, color=colour, s=20, label=cls)
ax.set_xlabel("Sodium (mmol/L)")
ax.set_ylabel("Age (years)")
ax.legend(title="Delirium")
ax.set_title("Training patients")
plt.show()
```

Delirium is common when sodium is **too low and when it is too high**, and
rarer in between. Fit the same kind of model as before, with age and sodium:

```{python}
line_model = LogisticRegression(C=np.inf)
line_model.fit(train_d[["age", "sodium"]], train_d["delirium"])

print("intercept:", line_model.intercept_)
print("weights (age, sodium):", line_model.coef_)
```

```{python}
#| code-fold: true
#| code-summary: "Code for this plot (optional)"
from matplotlib.colors import LinearSegmentedColormap

S, A = np.meshgrid(np.arange(114, 163.5, 0.5), np.arange(60, 98.5, 0.5))
grid_d = pd.DataFrame({"age": A.ravel(), "sodium": S.ravel()})
grid_d["sodium_dev2"] = (grid_d["sodium"] - 140) ** 2
blue_orange = LinearSegmentedColormap.from_list("bo", ["steelblue", "white", "darkorange"])

def delirium_map(model, columns, title):
    prob = model.predict_proba(grid_d[columns])[:, 1].reshape(S.shape)
    fig, ax = plt.subplots()
    im = ax.pcolormesh(S, A, prob, cmap=blue_orange, vmin=0, vmax=1, shading="auto")
    if prob.min() < 0.5 < prob.max():
        ax.contour(S, A, prob, levels=[0.5], colors="black")
    no, yes = test_d[test_d["delirium"] == "no"], test_d[test_d["delirium"] == "yes"]
    ax.scatter(no["sodium"], no["age"], marker="o", facecolors="none",
               edgecolors="black", s=20, label="test: no")
    ax.scatter(yes["sodium"], yes["age"], marker="^", color="black", s=20,
               label="test: yes")
    fig.colorbar(im, ax=ax, label="Probability of delirium")
    ax.set_xlabel("Sodium (mmol/L)")
    ax.set_ylabel("Age (years)")
    ax.set_title(title)
    ax.legend(loc="upper left", fontsize=8)
    plt.show()

delirium_map(line_model, ["age", "sodium"], "Logistic regression: age + sodium")
```

The weight for sodium is almost exactly 0, and the map has no boundary at all:
the probability never reaches 0.5, so the model says `no` for every patient.
A straight line has to put "high risk" on one side. Here the high-risk patients
are on **both** sides, so the best straight line the model can find is one that
hardly uses sodium.

#### Task 3a — Give the model a predictor it can use

How far sodium is from normal matters, not which direction. Make a new column,
the squared distance from 140, and add it to the model. The model is still a
logistic regression, linear in the predictors you give it, but one of those
predictors is now curved in sodium.

```{python}
#| eval: false
# Replace every ______ below, then run this cell.
train_d["sodium_dev2"] = (train_d["sodium"] - 140) ** 2
test_d["sodium_dev2"]  = (test_d["sodium"] - 140) ** 2

curve_columns = ["age", "sodium", "______"]
curve_model = LogisticRegression(C=np.inf)
curve_model.fit(train_d[curve_columns], train_d["delirium"])

print("weights (age, sodium, sodium_dev2):", curve_model.coef_)
```

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Stuck?
The third column is the name of the new column you just made.
:::

::: {.content-visible when-meta="show-solutions"}
::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}
## Worked answer
```{python}
train_d["sodium_dev2"] = (train_d["sodium"] - 140) ** 2
test_d["sodium_dev2"]  = (test_d["sodium"] - 140) ** 2

curve_columns = ["age", "sodium", "sodium_dev2"]
curve_model = LogisticRegression(C=np.inf)
curve_model.fit(train_d[curve_columns], train_d["delirium"])

print("weights (age, sodium, sodium_dev2):", curve_model.coef_)
```

The weight for `sodium_dev2` is positive (0.023): the further sodium is from
140, in either direction, the higher the log-odds of delirium. Age now has a
clear positive weight too (0.039).
:::
:::

```{python}
#| code-fold: true
#| code-summary: "Code for this plot (optional)"
delirium_map(curve_model, curve_columns,
             "Logistic regression: age + sodium + (sodium - 140)²")
```

A tree needs no new column: it can split on sodium twice.

```{python}
tree_model = DecisionTreeClassifier(max_depth=2, random_state=0)
tree_model.fit(train_d[["age", "sodium"]], train_d["delirium"])

print(export_text(tree_model, feature_names=["age", "sodium"]))
```

```{python}
#| code-fold: true
#| code-summary: "Code for this plot (optional)"
delirium_map(tree_model, ["age", "sodium"], "Decision tree: age + sodium")
```

How often is each model right on the 100 test patients, and what does each say
about an 80-year-old with a low, a normal and a high sodium?

```{python}
print(pd.DataFrame({
    "model": ["straight line", "with (sodium - 140)²", "tree", "always says no"],
    "accuracy": [line_model.score(test_d[["age", "sodium"]], test_d["delirium"]),
                 curve_model.score(test_d[curve_columns], test_d["delirium"]),
                 tree_model.score(test_d[["age", "sodium"]], test_d["delirium"]),
                 (test_d["delirium"] == "no").mean()]}))

patients = pd.DataFrame({"age": [80, 80, 80], "sodium": [126, 140, 154]})
patients["sodium_dev2"] = (patients["sodium"] - 140) ** 2
patients["straight_line"] = line_model.predict_proba(patients[["age", "sodium"]])[:, 1]
patients["with_squared"] = curve_model.predict_proba(patients[curve_columns])[:, 1]
patients["tree"] = tree_model.predict_proba(patients[["age", "sodium"]])[:, 1]
patients
```

::: {.callout-important appearance="simple"}
## Think about it
1. The straight-line model is right for 72% of the test patients. Is that a
   good model?
2. The straight-line model says sodium hardly matters. Is that true?
3. Describe the boundary of the model with the squared term, and of the tree.
:::

::: {.content-visible when-meta="show-solutions"}
::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}
## Worked answer
1. No. Always saying `no` is also right for 72%: the model says `no` to
   everyone and has learned nothing useful. Compare every accuracy with that
   baseline.
2. No. Sodium matters a great deal, but in both directions, which a straight
   line cannot express. An 80-year-old gets 0.33, 0.32 and 0.31 from the
   straight line whatever their sodium; the model with the squared term gives
   0.88, 0.08 and 0.91. A weight near 0 means "no straight-line relationship",
   not "no relationship".
3. The squared term gives two curved lines: delirium is predicted when sodium
   is below about 130 or above about 150, and the normal band narrows slightly
   with age (about 128 to 151 at 65, about 131 to 149 at 95). The tree gives
   three vertical bands of `yes`, `no`, `yes`, at sodium 130.5 and 149.5; it
   does not use age at all. (It also splits the low-sodium band at 127.5, but
   both halves still say `yes`.) Both are right for 88% of the test patients.
:::
:::

::: {.callout-important}
## Learning points
- The decision boundary is where the predicted probability equals the
  threshold. For a logistic regression that is where the log-odds equal
  $\log\big(t/(1-t)\big)$: 0 for a threshold of 0.5.
- A logistic regression's boundary is straight (flat) in its predictors.
  Changing the threshold moves it without changing its tilt.
- When the risk is high at both ends of a measurement, no straight line can
  separate the classes, and a weight near 0 can hide a strong relationship.
- A boundary can bend if you give the model a curved predictor, such as a
  squared term, or use a model that bends on its own, such as a tree.
:::

::: {.instructor}
**Teaching choice.** Part 1 links the map students saw in Exercise 4.1 to the
coefficients; Part 2 introduces the threshold, which Exercise 4.3 then puts
to use. No sensitivity or specificity here: that is Exercise 4.3. Parts 1 and 2 use the Day 4 dataset (`data/cvd_risk.csv`, simulated), in
which age and blood pressure carry similar weight, so the boundary is clearly
tilted. Part 3 uses a second
simulated dataset in which the risk is U-shaped in sodium. Both are generated
in `scripts/make_data.R` and described in `data/PROVENANCE.txt`.

**Expected values.** CVD data: 500 people, 176 with an event; training 400
(142), test 100 (34; baseline 0.66). Model: −14.22, age 0.1042, blood pressure
0.05292; accuracy 0.83. Boundary: blood pressure = 268.8 − 1.968 × age; age
75.6 at 120 mmHg, 55.3 at 160 mmHg; 10 mmHg ≈ 5.1 years. Age 70 / BP 130:
0.49; age 55 / BP 165: 0.56. Thresholds 0.3, 0.5, 0.7: log-odds −0.847, 0,
0.847; age at 140 mmHg 57.3, 65.4, 73.6; test patients called `yes` 52, 31,
15. Sodium data: 500
patients, 148 with delirium; training 400 (120 yes), test 100 (28 yes).
Straight line: −2.112, age 0.0228, sodium −0.0034; predicted probabilities
0.22 to 0.42, so `no` for everyone; accuracy 0.72 = baseline. With
`sodium_dev2`: −6.913, 0.0389, 0.0098, 0.0232; accuracy 0.88; boundary at age
80 sodium 129.6 and 150.0. Tree: R default 3 leaves (sodium < 130.5 → 0.82,
130.5–149.5 → 0.10, ≥ 149.5 → 0.80); Python `max_depth=2` 4 leaves (extra
split at 127.5, both `yes`); both 0.88. Patient aged 80, sodium 126 / 140 /
154: line 0.33 / 0.32 / 0.31, squared 0.88 / 0.08 / 0.91, tree 0.82 (Python
0.90, its extra leaf) / 0.10 / 0.80.

**Common failures.** (1) Forgetting that the boundary uses log-odds 0, not
probability 0, and solving β0 + β1 age + β2 BP = 0.5. (2) Dropping the
minus sign of the intercept in Task 1a. (3) In Task 3a, adding the column to
`train_d` but not to `test_d`, so prediction fails with a missing column.

**Timing.** Part 1 twenty minutes, Part 2 ten, Part 3 twenty.
